text: Units and standards. A physical quantity is defined by how it is measured or how it is calculated from other measurements. For example, distance measured using a meter stick or time measured with a stopwatch. Average speed is the total distance traveled divided by the travel time. Measurements of physical quantities are expressed in terms of standardized units. The foot was part of many local systems of units, but it was not standardized until 1959. It varied in length from city to city and even from trade to trade. Therefore, it's important to have a standardized length, for example, a meter, so that international science or manufacturing can operate smoothly. Two major units are used in the world. First, the SI units for the French system international dunité or metric system and second English units, i.e. the Imperial system. Systems of units are also referred to by just listing what they use for length, mass and time. For example, foot, pound, second or meter kilogram second. The metric system is agreed on by scientists and mathematicians. Engineers may use SAE units that measure tools in fractions of an inch rather than millimeters. SI units, base and derived units. The base quantities are measured using a system's base units. All other physical quantities are combinations of the base quantities where each are known as a derived quantity with its own derived unit. The derived units can only be as accurate and precise as the base units from which they are derived. There are seven base units that make up the international system of quantities, i.e. the I.S.Q. The course web page lists the units corresponding to the I.S.Q. base quantities. The course web page includes the table i.S.Q. base quantities, SI units and common Imperial equivalents. Examples of derived units are expressed as area square meters, volume cubic meters, or CC equals cubic centimeters equals milliliters in fluids, speed meters per second, density, kilograms per cubic meter, electric charge, ampere seconds, energy, electron volts. Units of time, length and mass. The second. For many years, the second was defined as 1 over 86,400 of a mean solar day. A new standard was introduced to define the second in terms of a non-varying physical phenomenon because the lunar and solar tides caused the Earth's rotation to slow over time. CCM atoms can vibrate in a steady way, allowing them to be easily observed and counted. In 1967, the second was redefined as the time required for 9,192,631,770 of these vibrations to occur. This level of precision is needed for global position satellites or GPS satellites to give you turn-by-turn directions due to time dilation in relativity. The meter. The meter has changed its definition over time, like the second, to become more precise. The meter was first defined in 1791 as 1 over 10 to the 7th of the distance from the equator to the North Pole. The measurement was improved in 1889 by redefining the meter as the distance between two engraved lines on a bar of platinum iridium kept in Paris. In 1960, it was redefined again as 1,650,763.73 wavelengths of light emitted by Krypton atoms. In 1983, the meter was given its current definition as the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1 over 299,792,458 of a second or 1 over c. The kilogram. Restate the mass 1.93 x 10 to the 13th kilograms using a metric prefix such that the resulting numerical value is a metric prefix. Metric prefix is bigger than 1, but less than 1,000. The model. We treat mass as a scalar physical quantity expressed as a numerical value multiplied by a unit. Metric prefix is in code powers of 10 and may not be combined or stacked. Therefore, the mass must first be rewritten using explicit powers of 10 before introducing a single appropriate prefix. Our goal is to select a metric prefix that produces a numerical value between 1 and 1,000 while representing the same physical mass. The math. The prefix kilo corresponds to a factor of 10 to the third. Rewriting the mass in grams gives 1.93 x 10 to the 13th kilograms equals 1.93 x 10 to the 13th kilograms times 10 to the third. The third grams per kilogram, which equals 1.93 x 10 to the 16th grams. From the metric prefix table, the power 10 to the 16th lies between peta, 10 to the 15th and Xa, 10 to the 18th. If we factor out 10 to the 15th, we obtain 1.93 x 10 to the 16th grams equals 1.93 x 10 to the 1st petagrams, which equals 19.3 petagrams. Alternatively, factoring out 10 to the 18th gives 1.93 x 10 to the 16th grams equals 1.93 x 10 to the minus 2nd x grams, which produces a numerical value less than 1 and therefore does not satisfy the requirement of the problem. The conclusion. The mass expressed using a single metric prefix with a numerical value between 1 and 1,000 is 1.93 x 10 to the 13th kilograms equals 19.3 petagrams.
